articles.title: Newsom on Stevens: Obviously it’s ‘sub-optimal’
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Sunday said Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) endorsement of Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was “sub-optimal.” Newsom spoke on “Decision Desk ’26 Midterm Preview” for an interview with 2WAY in collaboration with The Hill and NewsNation, where he was asked about the late endorsement. He…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Sunday said Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) endorsement of Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was “sub-optimal.”

Newsom spoke on “Decision Desk ’26 Midterm Preview” for an interview with 2WAY in collaboration with The Hill and NewsNation, where he was asked about the late endorsement. He called it an “October surprise of sorts” happening on Nov. 1.

“I don’t know enough about what ultimately led her to make that decision outside of what she said in that video , and she certainly has the right to do that, and I don’t condemn her on that basis,” Newsom said. “I don’t agree with her and made that point clear…”

“As I said, this was sub-optimal in every way, shape or form, and it’s an opportunity for you and your colleagues, and it’s about all you’ve got, with respect, in terms of this election,” he added. “Because it’s been pretty, pretty thin out there. It has been tough.”

Newsom said he didn’t have a double-standard for placing party over country or vice versa, “that’s why I’m not condemning her statement.”

“That’s her judgment, it was her determination. What’s difficult, and you know this Larry, she went 180 degrees overnight. So something else was going on there,” Newsom told conservative commentator Larry O’Connor.

The California Democrat noted that this incident was “exactly the conversation” Republicans want people to have, and he said Stevens was “successful in taking her eye off the ball.”

“And that’s why I understand party leadership condemning it and try to unify it,” he continued. “This moment on a critically important race –– we can look back and this may be that decisive moment.”

Stevens endorsed Rogers after she was due to attend a campaign event with El-Sayed before he dropped her from the event, according to sources familiar with the matter. Stevens appeared with Rogers at church Sunday to show her support two days before the midterm election.

The two Democrats faced-off in a bitter primary battle that ended with a narrow victory for El-Sayed. The two represented the divide within the Democratic Party, as both candidates differed over U.S. support for Israel after its years-long military campaign in Gaza.

Republicans were swift to praise Stevens for her endorsement, with the Republican National Committee (RNC) saying Michiganders “should take notice” and credited Rogers for building a “winning coalition” that included Democrats.

President Trump called the endorsement “BIG” and said he would “ love to have ” Stevens join the GOP. He said her actions were “the right thing” and “brave.”

Democrats lambasted the endorsement , with some calling it a betrayal. Michigan Democrats fumed, with Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel saying Stevens is no longer a “current member of the Michigan Democratic Party” and “nor will she be in the future.”

Mike Rogers (R) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race has outraged Democrats while giving Republicans welcome headlines and a glimmer of hope that they can flip the battleground seat. Democrats spewed anger over the move by Stevens, who joined Rogers at a…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) last-minute decision to endorse former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race has outraged Democrats while giving Republicans welcome headlines and a glimmer of hope that they can flip the battleground seat.

Democrats spewed anger over the move by Stevens , who joined Rogers at a Sunday church service in Detroit amid weekend sniping with El-Sayed, who had bested her in a bitter August primary, that ultimately imperiled a planned joint appearance alongside Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) and the Democratic Senate nominee.

In public, the party downplayed any impact the late development — a November surprise, if you will — would have on the crucial contest. They noted that many Michigan voters have already cast their ballots and raised doubts that Stevens would change many minds this close to Election Day.

But the news, coming at a time when Democratic hopes for a strong election, was hardly welcome, and Democratic leaders were outraged by what they viewed as treachery.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who supported Stevens in the primary, called her announcement a “despicable betrayal” while several members of Stevens’s official staff resigned in protest.

John Morgan, the longtime Democratic megadonor who donated to Stevens’s primary campaign, suggested her endorsement will help El-Sayed.

“What she demonstrated today is that she cares more about herself than the people in her state,” Morgan said. “She had a reputation for being mean and petty and proved it today.”

“She is now a washed up battle axe who has effectively retired from politics,” he added. “She is now officially radioactive.”

Michigan State Rep. Joe Tate (D), a former state House Speaker who also endorsed Stevens in the primary, called the episode “shocking and disappointing.”

“There are going to be some hard feelings after this,” he added. “That’s just a reality.”

But some members of the party were more circumspect. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) called the development “suboptimal” and “unfortunate” in an interview on 2WAY’s “The Morning Meeting,” stopping short of condemning the House Democrat.

El-Sayed and Rogers are locked in a tight race to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.), with a Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) polling average showing the Democratahead by close to 5 percentage points. DDHQ forecasts that El-Sayed has a 73 percent probability of winning the seat on Tuesday.

Recent public polling has shown El-Sayed’s lead largely hovering between 4 and 7 points. A Sunday poll from The New York Times and Siena University showed El-Sayed with an 11 point lead over Rogers.

The Great Lakes State is seen as one of Republicans’ best pick-up opportunities, and the GOP made it no secret they wanted to run against the progressive over Stevens during the primary.

Speaking to reporters alongside Stevens on Sunday, Rogers said he was “honored” to have her endorsement, calling it “courage in politics.”

Meanwhile, Stevens downplayed her reversal of support, saying “I’m not turning my back on Democrats,” while making it clear she was frustrated at El-Sayed for campaigning with controversial far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker during the primary and for disinviting her from the shared event planned for Sunday.

The two Democrats have been at odds over U.S. should support Israel amid the war in Gaza. The Hill has reached out to Stevens’ office for comment.

El-Sayed brushed off Stevens’ reversal of support, telling reporters flanked besides Clyburn and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) that he doesn’t think about her.

“This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from the government. I’m a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about,” he said, omitting Stevens and her fiancé, who is also supporting Rogers.

For Republicans, Stevens’s endorsement was a welcome development for the party, who believe even a small shift in support could make all the difference for their candidate.

“Mike Rogers continues to build a winning coalition of common-sense voters who Abdul El-Sayed has alienated by campaigning alongside Hasan Piker, who said ‘America deserves 9/11’ and failing to unequivocally condemn terrorist regimes like the Muslim Brotherhood and [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps],” Bernadette Breslin, a spokeswoman for the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, said in a statement.

Michigan Republican strategist Jason Cabel Roe said the news has shifted the momentum toward the Republican candidate.

“At the end of an election, you want to close on your message, and he’s done a very good job of controlling the message in his campaign,” Roe, who’s uninvolved in the Senate race, told The Hill. “And he now spends 48 hours explaining this away.”

Stevens is not the only prominent Democrat in Michigan who has not backed El-Sayed, Roe noted, citing former Michigan Democratic Party Chair Lon Johnson and Democratic fundraiser David Kramer, who chaired Stevens’s Senate campaign.

Still, her explicit endorsement of Rogers has angered and baffled Democrats, with some House Democrats telling Politico they’re mulling expelling her from their caucus. The congresswoman was quickly considered person non grata in Michigan, with the state party also removing her photo from its official website.

“Just when you think you’ve seen it all,” one Democratic strategist said. “To do it like this? It’s other level.”

Morgan predicted El Sayed would win “to make it insult to injury.” Another longtime Democratic donor agreed, “She’s become a total narcissist.”

Some Democrats, however, worried that Stevens endorsment could hurt El-Sayed with less than 48 hours until Election Day.

“Why do we always have this ability to f— s— up?” a second Democratic strategist said. “Every single time, count on us to f— it up.”

“All she had to do was manage to keep it together for a couple more days,” they continued. “Somehow, it’s what we always do.”

It’s unclear how Stevens’s eleventh-hour move will ultimately affect the final vote for El-Sayed. Michigan pollster Richard Czuba suggested that if the polling is accurately capturing the dynamics of the race, her endorsment is unlikely to hurt Democrats.

Although the news “would certainly help energize Republicans a bit,” Czuba noted that President Trump’s low approval ratings bogging down the GOP will matter more.

“In our numbers, if you disapprove of Donald Trump, 83 percent of those voters are going to Abdul. If you approve of Trump, 92 percent of those voters are going to Rogers,” Czuba said. “That’s the dividing line. It’s not Haley Stevens.”

Regardless of Tuesday’s outcome, however, Democrats see a dim political future for Stevens.

“I’m generally willing to show a lot of grace to candidates who lose their primary,” said Steve Schale, a veteran Democratic strategist. “She could have kept her mouth shut — which I’d understand, but instead she chose to end her career.”

articles.title: Newsom on possible Democrat ‘tsunami’ on Election Day: ‘That’s a word I haven’t used lightly’
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Sunday said there’s a chance that there could be a massive Democratic victory, or a “blue tsunami,” on Election Day, and that there is momentum behind the party to reclaim one or both chambers of Congress. “It could be that blue tsunami, but you make that legitimate and obvious…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Sunday said there’s a chance that there could be a massive Democratic victory, or a “blue tsunami,” on Election Day, and that there is momentum behind the party to reclaim one or both chambers of Congress.

“It could be that blue tsunami, but you make that legitimate and obvious point,” Newsom said on “ Decision Desk ’26: Midterm Preview ,” hosted by 2WAY in collaboration with The Hill and NewsNation, to moderator and journalist Mark Halperin. “The margins in those Senate races suggest that, obviously, maybe it won’t be on that side of the aisle, as well.”

“We’re all going to be experts in hindsight. It will all be obvious –– what’s happened –– in 48 hours. But I just –– that tsunami. That’s a word I haven’t used lightly and it’s a word that I’m sharing privately and publicly,” he told Halperin and his co-hosts for the evening, Democratic strategist Kevin Walling and conservative commentator Larry O’Connor.

The governor added, “I just feel it everywhere I’ve been. These things seems to be teed up despite the headwinds of today in Michigan,” referring to Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) endorsement of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), who is up for reelection on Tuesday, appeared after Newsom and dismissed any chances of a “tsunami.” He said there was a “frustration” at the state and national levels against Democrats.

“People are feeling the pain,” he said. “I listened to Gavin Newsom. It’s as if he hasn’t been in elected office for 30 years though. California and New York are two of the most expensive states anywhere in the country because of the policy decisions that they make…”

“And so I don’t think the blue tsunami, as Gavin Newsom predicts, is going to be reaching New York in terms of my congressional seat,” Lawler later added.

Polling estimates show that Democrats are primed to likely win the House on Tuesday. The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) holds an 83-percent probability that Democrats win the House, who will need at least three seats to win a majority.

Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats to win the Senate. DDHQ estimates that they have a 62-percent chance to bring the Senate under Democratic control.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) on Sunday said there will be “debate” within the GOP about the MAGA movement should they suffer losses in the midterms. He cited “Ronald Reagan principles” as something the party has backed away from during President Trump’s two administrations.

“I think the Republican Party, I think America yearns for those principles … And I surely would like to see a debate, and I know I want to be a part of it,” he said on CNN.

Trump, who has seen his approval rating plummet across several polls over his handling on the economy and the Iran war, has called on Republicans to “ pretend ” as though he is on the ballot to increase voter turnout, which is generally lower in each midterm cycle.

articles.title: Democrats edge out Republicans in 7 heated Senate races: NYT polls
articles.summary: Democrats are edging out their Republican counterparts in seven competitive Senate races ahead of Tuesday’s election, though the majority of them show statistical ties between the two parties, according to new polling. Polling released by The New York Times and Siena University on Sunday show Democrats holding an 11-point lead in the Michigan race, a…
articles.body:
Democrats are edging out their Republican counterparts in seven competitive Senate races ahead of Tuesday’s election, though the majority of them show statistical ties between the two parties, according to new polling.

Polling released by The New York Times and Siena University on Sunday show Democrats holding an 11-point lead in the Michigan race, a 7-point lead in Texas, a 6-point lead in Maine, 5-point leads in Kansas and Ohio, a 2-point lead in Alaska and a 1-point lead in Iowa.

Only Senate Democratic candidates Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas polled outside the full margin of error spread, meaning the Democrats were statistically tied in the other five races.

The November election is two days out, and Democrats are vying for a rare opportunity to flip the Senate. Decision Desk HQ forecasts the party has a 62 percent chance of taking the upper chamber this week.

President Trump’s declining approval ratings, high costs of living associated with the Iran war and the tariff war with Canada in addition to concerns over candidate quality have put an increasing number of Senate seats in play for Democrats. The party needs four seats to win back the upper chamber.

One clear trend across the seven polls was that every Democrat led their Republican rival among independent voters, though that lead varied between single and double digits depending on the race. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) held a 9-point lead among the bloc while Maine Senate Democratic candidate Troy Jackson held an 11-point lead.

Talarico, meanwhile, held the largest lead among independents, besting Republican Ken Paxton by 30 points.

Democratic candidates also were able to better shore up their base, including 2024 supporters of former Vice President Harris, compared to Republicans and 2024 Trump voters.

What’s kept the race tighter in Iowa is the fact that Republican Ashley Hinson has been able to narrowly edge out Democrat Josh Turek among voters between the ages of 30 and 64 years old, though Turek holds a 5-point lead among voters aged 65 and older. Ninety-three percent of Democrats support Turek while a similar 90 percent of Republicans say the same about Hinson.

Democrats received an unwelcome November surprise when Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) reversed her endorsement of El-Sayed and instead backed GOP nominee Mike Rogers on Sunday.

She downplayed the move, saying she wasn’t “turning my back on Democrats” while the progressive brushed off the Rogers endorsement, saying he was more concerned about the rest of the state than her and her fiancé, who also endorsed Rogers. While some Democrats don’t think it will change the trajectory of the race before Tuesday, leaders of the party saw it as an unhelpful distraction.

The polling from The New York Times and Siena University was conducted between Oct. 23 and Nov. 1. In Alaska, 610 voters were surveyed with a margin of error of 4.8 points. In Iowa, 705 voters were surveyed with a margin of error of 4.4 points. In Kansas, 736 voters were surveyed with a margin of error of 4.1 points. In Maine, 714 voters were surveyed with a margin of error of 4.3 points. In Michigan, 1,011 voters were surveyed, including on Sunday, with 3.6-point margin of error. In Ohio, 717 voters were surveyed, with a 4.2-point margin of error. In Texas, 1,215 voters were surveyed with a 3.3-point margin of error.

articles.title: Collins accuses Schumer of pushing attack ads filled with 'outright lies' in tight Maine race
articles.summary: Collins said Democrats are using a national political strategy to distract voters from local issues, while the latest Fox News poll shows her Maine Senate race tied at 49%.
articles.body: Sen. Susan Collins on Sunday blasted Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Party over what she described as a wave of false attack ads targeting her and other Republican candidates, saying she has never seen a campaign with "so many outright lies." She made the remarks during an interview with Fox News on Sunday, just two days before Election Day in Maine, where she is seeking reelection in a closely watched race against Democratic rival Troy Jackson. According to the latest Fox News poll, the two candidates are tied at 49%. Collins accused Democrats of following "Chuck Schumer's playbook," pointing to attack ads she said were nearly identical to those targeting other Republican lawmakers. MANCHIN CALLS SCHUMER 'CRAZY' FOR TRYING TO OUST GOP SENATOR IN CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN "One of the outrageous, completely false ads against me had to do with Jeffrey Epstein. And it turns out, in talking to two of my colleagues who are in tough races, that they had virtually identical ads run against them. So this is part of Chuck Schumer's playbook," she said. "There are a lot of differences between my opponent and me, but I've never seen a campaign with so many outright lies. It's very frustrating," she added. Collins further accused Democrats of trying to shift the focus away from local issues and toward divisive national political battles. "It's certainly an attempt by my opponent and Chuck Schumer and their allies to nationalize this race," she said. SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY Turning to her own campaign, Collins portrayed herself as a bipartisan lawmaker willing to work across party lines, arguing that the Senate needs more centrists as moderates increasingly leave Washington. "Unfortunately, a lot of them have given up and retired or decided they just didn't want to run again. And that's one reason I am running again," she said. "We need more people who are willing to work across party lines. That is really important," she said. FOX NEWS POLL: NAIL-BITER IN MAINE SENATE RACE She also described herself as the "most independent senator on either side of the aisle," pointing to her voting record and saying her decisions are based on what she believes is right, rather than who occupies the White House or what President Donald Trump supports. "There's this phony figure out there that I voted with President Trump 95% of the time. That's based on a sample of only 30% of the votes. If you look at a broader sample of 90% of the vote, that drops significantly to like 72%. And I voted against the president's policies 138 times," she said. While Jackson previously told Fox News that he believes he has a "good shot" at defeating Collins, the longtime Republican senator touted strong voter support and said she is more optimistic than ever about her reelection chances. articles.title: Stevens defends endorsing Rogers during tense CNN interview
articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Sunday defended her endorsement of Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in a tense interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper. Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in a bitter primary, had assured Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) in a phone call Saturday night that she supported El-Sayed after the…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) on Sunday defended her endorsement of Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in a tense interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper.

Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in a bitter primary, had assured Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) in a phone call Saturday night that she supported El-Sayed after the senior lawmaker asked Stevens not to attend a church event with the candidate Sunday morning.

Cooper asked Stevens what had changed overnight.

“Well, look, this is just a weight off my shoulders, OK?” Stevens said. “Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier. I was trying to help, I endorsed him … There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee. And they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in,’ or ‘This is a campaign you don’t belong in.'”

“And I’ve never cast a present vote in the Congress,” she continued. “I’m making a decision here and that’s just where I landed on this. I woke up this morning, clear-eyed, fresh and focused on what was in my heart, and that’s that.”

Cooper pressed Stevens about the phone call. The lawmaker said she “wasn’t on the phone I think that late, but I know Debbie’s always working around the clock.” She said she was “with [her] thoughts” and “writing things out” before bringing up “this level of anger, and the things that we are seeing.”

She stated her loyalty to the party and said “nothing with me changed, Anderson.” Cooper pressed her again on his question.

“Oh Anderson, you certainly weren’t on the phone with me at midnight, and I don’t think I was on the phone either,” Stevens said. “But I have great respect for Congresswoman Dingell, and you know, she is a pillar…”

Cooper repeated the question twice as Stevens continued speaking before contextualizing what happened and asking the question a third time.

“Anderson, this is a broader point about what’s going on in our party,” Stevens said.

“It’s actually not, it’s just a question about why you would change your mind,” Cooper interjected.

Stevens said she has not cast her vote yet, prompting Cooper to ask, “So you might change your mind again?” Stevens said her mind was “made up” and that she still loves the Democratic Party “a whole lot.”

Cooper then pointed to a post on the social platform X from Stevens against giving “MAGA another Senate seat in November” and asked “why is it OK now?”

“Well, why is it OK to have the Democratic Party, and a top nominee, ejecting –– you know, this type, or injecting, rather, this type of anger and lack of kindness? That’s all,” Stevens replied, before later saying it sounded like Cooper was upset with her.

“No, I’m not,” he said. “You’re really not answering any of my questions so it’s somewhat frustrating.”

The back-and-forth continued, with Stevens saying she could not condone El-Sayed campaigning with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker and pointed to comments made by him and Piker’s uncle, “The Young Turks” co-founder Cenk Uygur, as reason for people to “feel hurt” by El-Sayed’s campaign.

“Look, I appreciate all the introspection on how I make my decisions and how I reached this moment,” Stevens at one point said.

Cooper asked about staffers leaving Stevens’s congressional office over the endorsement. She called her team “incredible” and that she was “under transition,” as she is leaving at the end of her term.

“These are great individuals who I care a lot about and, certainly, they’re free to share their views on this,” she said. “I am not trying to upset anyone.”

Stevens dismissed President Trump’s praise toward her endorsement, telling Cooper that she voted to impeach the president twice.

The interview reached a long pause, followed by Stevens accusing Cooper of editorializing while he asked her about the call again. The interview ended shortly after.

Dingell appeared next, calling the interview between Cooper and Stevens “one of the most painful interviews I have ever watched.” She said that the flurry since the endorsement “has all become a distraction” but that it was “backfiring,” saying El-Sayed has “raised more money today, more than a million dollars.”

Cooper asked if the two spoke. Dingell said they spoke late Saturday night and said many others “were embarrassed” by the news on Sunday morning. He asked the senior lawmaker if Stevens said on their phone call that she was not going to endorse Rogers.

“Yes, she did,” Dingell said. “Multiple times.”

Dingell said she “loves” Stevens and operates differently than her as a lawmaker and emphasized the division seen on the campaign trail. But she urged Democrats to vote for their party candidates.

“By the end of the day, I thought Abdul was going to win, but I felt a shift just being out, as I always am, this afternoon,” she said. “So, I think this race is going to be close. Anybody watching should not think that they shouldn’t go to the polls, that their votes don’t matter –– but I think it’s been a very difficult day and it’s been very painful for many people to watch.”

articles.title: Trump makes final weekend campaign push ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: The US president rallied in states that Republicans previously won - showcasing how tight Tuesday's elections could be in determining control of Congress.
articles.body:
In the last weekend before the pivotal midterm elections, Donald Trump has made a final pitch to voters in hopes of keeping Republicans in control of the US Congress.

Trump held rallies in Florida, Iowa and Kansas - states he won in past elections - in a sign of Republicans' defensive stance in Tuesday's elections.

Facing voter frustration over rising prices, particularly fuel, Trump sought to tamp down such concerns and shift focus on attacking Democrats, saying they would "bankrupt" families if elected.

Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance at winning at least partial control of Congress, which would act as a check on Trump's power and upend the last two years of his presidency.

Trump has been campaigning non-stop across the country ahead of the election - even in areas that were once thought to be safe Republican strongholds.

Throughout the weekend, Trump made the case for his party at rallies in Kansas, Florida and Iowa as well as at tele-rallies for candidates in states including Michigan, Ohio and Pennsylvania.

In previous years, Trump easily won Florida, Iowa and Kansas - once considered reliably Republican states - but the president's visits there in the final days of his election drive highlighted just how competitive these states have become in determining control of Congress.

Trump told supporters he had transformed the country, saying Democrats had left the US in a "dark age" but under his command, "we quickly turned it into the golden age of America".

Trump is facing a backlash over the cost of living. Prices have gone up , particularly for fuel, groceries and health care, since the war in Iran began over eight months ago. At these rallies, Trump appeared to have two aims: to change the subject from those issues and use fear to turn out the Republican vote.

At rallies in Florida and Iowa, he highlighted his policies on trade and immigration and said if Democrats were given power, they would "open the border", "bankrupt your family", "take away your guns" and "mutilate your children". He played video montages of Democrats criticising ICE and supporting transgender rights.

In the room at the rallies, supporters cheered, but there has also been disquiet among some Republicans over Trump's appeal with more moderate voters.

Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said this weekend that he was "very confident" his party was on course to win control of the House of Representatives, as senior Democrats including former President Barack Obama made final appeals to voters.

A forecasting tool from Harvard University that analyses and compiles multiple polls and historical data suggests that Democrats have a 96% chance of taking the House and a 76% chance of taking the Senate.

A national poll from NBC News posted this weekend suggests that registered voters prefer a Democrat-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, leading Republicans 52% to 45%.

But along with the last-push campaign stops, this weekend featured a dramatic turn in the Senate race in Michigan - a tightly contested seat currently held by Democrats.

Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost the Democratic Senate nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.

The move led to widespread condemnation from fellow Democrats and praise from Republicans, including Trump who called her "very brave".

In Alaska, home to another crucial Senate race, a judge on Sunday dismissed an attempt by the Trump administration to delay certifying election results if the Republican incumbent candidate loses due to two candidates appearing on the ballot with the same name.

In the lead up to the election, Trump and his administration have repeatedly cast doubt on both the credibility and security of the vote, despite evidence showing voter fraud is rare. The justice department has launched investigations or demanded votes be set aside in multiple US states.

The stakes are high for Trump, as midterm election results are seen as a measure of how satisfied Americans are with a president's performance.

In most midterm elections, the party that holds the White House typically loses seats in Congress to the opposing party - meaning Trump's Republican party has the most to lose.

Republicans, who currently hold a slim majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate, don't want to relinquish their party's majority in Congress, as losing any seats would hinder their ability to pass laws and shape policies.

Democrats, however, are keen to gain control from Republicans. Holding a majority would enable them to challenge Trump's agenda, give them investigative powers over his administration, and could also help them showcase their vision for America ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

For lawmakers, it's all about gaining or maintaining power and control, but it's Americans who will feel the impacts of their policies.

Who gets elected at the city, state, and federal level affects many aspects of voters' everyday lives, including the cost of gas, rising inflation and grocery prices, healthcare and abortion access, income and property taxes, and immigration.

articles.title: Dingell says Stevens defending Rogers endorsement on CNN was ‘one of the most painful interviews I’ve ever watched’
articles.summary: Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) on Sunday called Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, where she defended her endorsement of former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in Michigan’s Senate race, “one of the most painful interviews I’ve ever watched.” Cooper, after a tense exchange with Stevens about why she changed her mind to endorse…
articles.body:
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) on Sunday called Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper , where she defended her endorsement of former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in Michigan’s Senate race, “one of the most painful interviews I’ve ever watched.”

Cooper, after a tense exchange with Stevens about why she changed her mind to endorse Rogers over Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D), quickly apologized to Dingell for having her on right after Stevens without Dingell knowing.

“First of all, I’m going to say I’m not sure I would have done this if I had known she was going to be on immediately before me,” Dingell began. “That was one of the most painful interviews I’ve ever watched. I have been worried about her all last week. She’s a human being. I’ve had multiple conversations with her. I’m far from being the only one that has.”

Dingell said she worried this would be a “distraction” against electing Democrats who will address growing concerns over the cost of living, and that the focus on Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers left Dingell “sad.”

“And I think that this is backfiring,” she later said. “Abdul has raised more money today, more than a million dollars, talking to different people that have been at different polls … By the end of the day, I thought Abdul was going to win, but I felt a shift just being out, as I always am, this afternoon. So I think this race is going to be close.”

Cooper asked if El-Sayed should have done anything different, as sources close to the matter said the candidate asked Stevens not to attend a campaign event at a church with him Sunday morning.

“I’m actually the one that called her and said, ‘This has become a distraction,'” Dingell said. “…I don’t know what I wish. This has been a very difficult week to watch, and I know that Michigan is tired of the drama, that they’re really worried about everyday issues.”

Cooper later asked Dingell if Stevens did say she would not endorse Rogers during their call Saturday night, a question the CNN anchor asked Stevens several times in their interview.

“Yes, she did,” Dingell said. “Multiple times.”

The endorsement stirred controversy, with members of Stevens’s staff resigning and Michigan Democrats fuming at the lawmaker. Other Democrats called the move a “betrayal,” with Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) calling it “insane.”

“There’s a fascist dictator in the White House,” she wrote on the social platform X . “Mike Rogers is a racist who supports a nationwide abortion ban AND the fascist dictator. With this move, Haley Stevens is no longer a Democrat.”

National Republicans, including President Trump, celebrated Stevens’s endorsement . The president said he would “ love to have ” her join the GOP.

articles.title: Trump leans into Islamophobia and conspiracy in last-ditch campaign rallies
articles.summary: Trump attacks Muslim politicians Abdul El-Sayed and Ilhan Omar in his two last rallies on the campaign trail.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has doubled down on Islamophobic rhetoric and conspiracy theories about the Democratic Party at campaign events in Iowa and Kansas, days before the US votes in crucial midterm elections that will decide who controls Congress during Trump’s last two years as president.

The president repeated his claim that Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic US Senate hopeful from Michigan, is a “jihadist” at both rallies on Sunday, and joked that if he gets elected, the Senate will have to install metal detectors to scan him before he enters the building.

“We’ll have a hundred senators, and most of them will go directly [into the Senate]… We’re gonna have to get a special metal detector for Abdul,” Trump said, drawing laughter from the crowd.

He also repeated unfounded claims that El-Sayed is a member of the transnational Muslim Brotherhood, branches of which the US has deemed foreign “terrorist” organisations.

At both events, Trump repeatedly urged his supporters to make sure they go out and vote, asking them to “pretend I’m on the ballot”, as he sought to energise Republican voters ahead of what polling suggests could be a bruising election for the party.

The two rallies were cancelled last week but were suddenly rescheduled . They will be Trump’s final travelling events before the election.

Both speeches were interrupted multiple times by hecklers.

In Iowa, the president said he would “love” Democratic Representative Haley Stevens, who lost to Abdul El-Sayed in the primaries, to switch parties, after she endorsed El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

At both rallies, he took aim at US Representative for Minnesota Ilhan Omar, whom Trump claims, without evidence, was previously married to her brother and had children with him.

In Kansas, Trump attacked the Democratic Senate hopeful Adam Hamilton, a church pastor , for his support for trans rights, and called him a “stiff” who reads his sermons from teleprompters.

The US-Israel war on Iran, the cost of living, immigration, perceived media bias against him, and the administration of former President Joe Biden also featured heavily in Trump’s two speeches.

While Iowa and Kansas are represented mostly by Republican lawmakers, polling suggests Democrats could flip both states.

Kansas has five federal congressional seats up for election in the midterms: one Senate seat and all four House seats. The state last elected a Democratic senator in 1932.

In Iowa, the Senate race is too close to call, but polling suggests that two Iowan state representative seats up for grabs are leaning Democrat.

The US will vote in the midterm elections on November 3.

articles.title: Senator Chris Murphy suffered a stroke and is expected to recover
articles.summary: The Connecticut Democrat had been campaigning around the country for Democrats on the ballot this midterm election.
articles.body:
US Senator Chris Murphy has been taken to hospital after suffering a stroke on Saturday, his team has said.

The 53-year-old Connecticut Democrat was at his son's hockey game when he began feeling "numbness in his arm" and was taken to hospital, his team said in a statement shared with US media. It was discovered in hospital that he had experienced a stroke.

"The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery," his team said.

Murphy, who is not up for re-election this midterms cycle, has been campaigning around the country in support of fellow Democrats who are on the ballot this year.

The stakes are high for his party, which is trying to wrest control of Congress away from Republicans, who currently hold the majority in both the House and Senate.

Murphy has served in the Senate since 2013 and was previously in the House of Representatives. The Democrat - who is considered a possible 2028 White House candidate - has championed progressive causes including affordable health care, international human rights, and gun safety.

He has recently made stops in Michigan, Minnesota and Florida to attend campaign events for Democratic candidates on the ballot, and he had been scheduled to travel to New Hampshire on Sunday.

Several other Senators have experienced strokes in the last few years, including Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen in 2022, New Mexico Democrat Ben Ray Lujan the same year, and Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman.

Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, the former majority leader, was out of the Capitol for months earlier this year after he had a bad fall and was taken to hospital.

Fetterman offered his well wishes for Murphy and his family in a social media post on Sunday.

"As someone who survived a near-fatal stroke, I understand all too well how much this impacts your life," Fetterman wrote on X. "My family is rooting for Chris and his family for a full and speedy recovery."
